humanities_role_explanation: The benchmark evaluates disciplinary competence in Art History, targeting stylistic, iconographic, and contextual visual understanding using human-authored educational exam materials rather than treating artworks as generic visual data.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Multi-modal visual question answering combining low-to-medium resolution artwork images (paintings) with text-based questions across seven formats.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Evaluates art-historical capabilities ranging from factual recognition of styles, artists, and techniques to deeper visual reasoning and iconographic interpretation. It tests these via multiple-choice (single and multiple selection), true/false statement classification, in-text word positioning, closed/open completion (fill-in-the-blanks), and error identification in art-historical prose.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: The benchmark is explicitly scoped to evaluating Art History knowledge and visual reasoning.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluated 12 models including GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 Mini/Nano, Gemini 3.1 Pro/3.5 Flash, Claude 4.6 (Opus/Sonnet) and 4.5 (Haiku), Qwen3-VL, Mistral Large 3, and Pixtral Large.

quantitative_metrics.note: Uses exact match accuracy, F1 score, statement/element/blank accuracy, and Classical Test Theory (CTT) point-biserial correlation for item discrimination.

summary: This paper introduces EduArt, an educational-level benchmark containing 871 human-authored questions in Italian and English drawn from secondary school and AP Art History exams. The authors leverage Classical Test Theory to assess the difficulty and discrimination of items across seven distinct formats, revealing how model performance varies. Crucially, the study compares a default answer-only condition against a reasoning-elicitation condition to examine how written justification affects accuracy.
key_findings: While top-tier models approach ceiling performance on multiple-choice formats (exceeding 94% accuracy), their performance collapses on production-based tasks like open completion (falling to 23.9% for Claude Opus 4.6) and error identification (dropping to 6.2% for Claude Sonnet 4.6). Additionally, the requirement to provide written justifications yields model-family-dependent outcomes, consistently improving Claude models while degrading GPT and Gemini performance.
facets_explanation: The reference answers are derived from pre-existing educational assessments: Italian secondary-school exercises (MyZanichelli) and US Advanced Placement Art History examinations (2013-2024), representing standardized answer keys. Answering these questions requires extensive art-historical, stylistic, and contextual knowledge that is not present in the image or question text alone. Because the dataset relies on established educational curricula with singular correct answers, it does not explicitly address community-dependent variations or interpretive disagreements among annotators.
results_explanation: The benchmark reports that 'models exceeding 94 percent on multiple choice can fall to 23.9 percent on open completion (Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2 percent on error identification (Claude Sonnet 4.6)', representing a maximum format gap of 88.1 percentage points (rounded to 88) for Claude Sonnet 4.6. The best performing model on the primary macro-average accuracy metric is 'Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview' with '82.8 %'. No quantified human baseline is reported. A systematic language asymmetry is identified via logistic regression, showing that 'Language: Italian' questions have significantly lower odds of being answered correctly than English ones, with an odds ratio of '0.459' (p < .001).
